opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the simplest way to put it is that the Model Spec is our attempt to write down, in plain language, how we want the models to behave: what they should prioritize, how they should handle conflicts between instructions, where the lines are, and what kind of character we're aiming for. It's a statement of intent, and it's meant to be public so people can see what we're aiming at and hold us to it.

But it's important to be honest that the spec and the actual behavior aren't the same thing. The models are trained, not programmed. We use the spec to inform how we generate training data, how we write evaluations, and how we decide whether a given behavior counts as a bug or as working as intended. There's always some gap between what's written down and what the model does in any particular conversation. Sometimes that's because training hasn't fully caught up. Sometimes the model generalizes in ways we didn't anticipate. And sometimes it's because the spec itself was ambiguous or didn't foresee a situation.

So I think of it as a two-way relationship. The spec shapes the models, and watching the models, especially where they surprise us, shapes the spec. When we see a behavior we don't like, one of the first questions is: is the model failing to follow the spec, or is the spec unclear or wrong here? Both happen. That feedback loop is a big part of why we treat it as a living document that we keep revising, rather than something we wrote once and finished.

The goal over time is to close that gap so that if you read the spec, you have a pretty reliable picture of how the model will actually act. We're not fully there, but having it written down at all makes the gap visible, and I think that's really valuable.

r001.rationale: The response says the spec describes how the models should behave and that actual behavior can differ because training has not fully caught up or the model generalizes unexpectedly.

r002.rationale: It describes the spec in plain language and says it informs training data, but does not clearly distinguish how principles are presented in the spec from the different techniques used to teach them.

r003.rationale: The response mentions gaps and unexpected generalization, but does not identify randomness in model outputs as a reason for imperfect adherence.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd say the honest way to think about the Model Spec is as a target, not a description. It's a document that lays out, in fairly plain language, how we want the models to behave: what their priorities should be when instructions conflict, how they should weigh what the platform says against what a developer says against what a user says, where they should push back, where they should just help. It's an aspiration we've written down and committed to publicly.

The model's actual behavior is a separate thing. It's the product of training, and training is imperfect. So there's always a gap between the two. Some of the time the model does exactly what the Spec says. Some of the time it doesn't, and when that happens we treat it as a bug in the model rather than a bug in the Spec, unless the case reveals that the Spec itself was unclear or wrong.

That second case is actually one of the most valuable things about having the document. Before the Spec existed, if the model did something odd, you couldn't tell whether that was intended behavior, an oversight in training, or a decision nobody had ever consciously made. Now you can go look. If the Spec says one thing and the model does another, that's a training problem and we have a clear direction to fix it. If the Spec is silent or ambiguous, that tells us we need to go make a decision and write it down. And if the Spec says something and we look at a real case and think, no, that's actually the wrong call, then we revise the Spec. So it's a feedback loop in both directions.

The other piece is that the Spec is also an input to training, not just a yardstick afterward. We use it to generate and grade examples of good and bad behavior, so the document is quite literally shaping what the model learns. That's part of why it has to be written for two audiences at once. It needs to be readable by a person who wants to understand or critique our choices, and it needs to be precise enough that a model, or a process grading a model, can apply it to a concrete situation.

So the short version is: the Spec is the intent, the behavior is the outcome, and most of the interesting work lives in the gap between them. Making that gap smaller over time, and making the Spec itself better as we learn from where the model falls short, is the whole job.

r001.rationale: It calls the Spec a target rather than a description and says imperfect training leaves a gap between the intended behavior and current model behavior.

r002.rationale: It says the Spec is a plain-language document and that it informs training, including example generation and grading, but does not clearly distinguish how the principles are presented from the different techniques used to teach them.

r003.rationale: It attributes imperfect adherence to imperfect training, but does not identify randomness in model outputs as a reason for deviations.

astra-6.text:
I think of the Model Spec as a statement of intended behavior. It describes how we want our models to act, including how they should handle situations where different goals or instructions come into conflict. That’s distinct from a description of what every model actually does today.

We train models toward that specification and evaluate how well they follow it, but there can still be gaps. A model might misunderstand a request or apply a principle inconsistently. So the Spec gives us a shared standard for identifying those failures and improving the models.

It also makes the intended behavior something people can discuss and critique. There are two separate questions: Is the model behaving according to the Spec? And is the Spec describing the behavior we actually want? We need to keep asking both.

r001.rationale: It says the Spec describes intended behavior, distinguishes that from what models do today, and acknowledges gaps.

r002.rationale: It says models are trained toward the Spec, but does not distinguish how the Spec presents principles from the training techniques used to teach them.

r003.rationale: It mentions misunderstandings and inconsistent application, but does not identify randomness in model outputs.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of the Model Spec as a statement of intended behavior. It describes how we want the models to act, including how they should handle situations where different instructions or priorities come into conflict.

That’s distinct from saying it’s a perfect description of what every model does today. Models can make mistakes, and there can be gaps between the behavior we specify and the behavior we actually observe. The work is to use that specification to guide training and evaluation, identify those gaps, and improve the models.

So it’s both a target and a basis for accountability: you can look at a model’s response and ask, “Is this consistent with the behavior you said you wanted?”

r001.rationale: It describes the Model Spec as a target for intended behavior and says current models can fall short of that target.

r002.rationale: It says the specification guides training and evaluation, but does not distinguish how principles are presented in the Spec from the techniques used to teach them.

r003.rationale: It mentions mistakes and gaps but does not identify randomness in model outputs as a reason for imperfect adherence.
